paragraphs.source_en: In my opinion, the Epipalaeolithic culture was a result of the new climatic and environmental conditions, unknown in the final Late Pleistocene. This change not only caused a new way of life for huntergatherers but probably a new way of thinking. Speaking about religion Goodman (1988: 8) states that the world's religious systems appear to be closely related but in some cases the differences are so sharp that a powerful disruptive force must have occurred. Goodman (1988) believes that this disruption resulted from a change in people's interaction with their habitat, leading to an important modification in lifestyle, which also affected religious behaviour. Interaction with habitat represents the main force in the complicated system that is culture and the components of culture are its dependent variables (Goodman 1988).

paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the Central Sahara, I propose that the "powerful disruptive force" was the change in the climate and environment, so marked that it caused the alteration of the religious beliefs of the Early Holocene Epipalaeolithic hunter-gatherers. The new beliefs and ideology were then expressed in the Round Head paintings.

paragraphs.source_en: If the new way of thinking was the result of new conditions, it means that major variations occurred in the very beginning of the climatic optimum, shortly before the 10th millennium BP during the Epipalaeolithic period. In this period new groups of hunter-gatherers may have reached the mountainous regions, contributing to the development of art and culture and possibly interacting with the previous groups living in the mountains since the Late Pleistocene. This period of change would incite the origin and spread of the Round Head art, and the Mesolithic would be the continuation of that new era. However, the ideology, religious beliefs and the art, although in an innovated form, would be deeply rooted in the earlier Late Pleistocene cultural heritage.
